sections.title: Computers around us
sections.description: Computers big and small, the computers hiding inside everyday things, robots, and how devices join together in networks and the internet.

sections.title: Following and giving instructions
sections.description: Algorithms as steps in the right order, turning steps into blocks, giving directions, and finding and fixing mistakes.

sections.title: Data and staying safe
sections.description: Sorting and counting data, tally marks, pictograms and block graphs, and keeping yourself safe online.

questions.question: Which of these is a computer?
questions.options: a wooden spoon | a smartphone | a paper book | a football
questions.explanation: A smartphone is a little computer — it plays games, takes photos and much more, as well as making calls.

questions.question: What does a program (also called an app) do?
questions.options: It cleans the computer screen | It tells the computer what to do | It keeps the computer warm | It makes the computer heavier
questions.correctAnswer: It tells the computer what to do
questions.explanation: A program, or app, is what tells the computer what to do — a computer only does what its program says.

questions.question: Which computer folds up like a book so you can carry it with you?
questions.options: a desktop | a laptop | a keyboard | a television
questions.explanation: A laptop folds up like a book, so you can carry it — a desktop is big and stays on a desk.

questions.question: Which of these has a little computer hiding inside it?
questions.options: a plain ball | a washing machine | a metal spoon | a wooden chair
questions.explanation: A washing machine has a little computer hiding inside that controls it. Plain, simple things like a chair, a ball or a spoon have no computer.

questions.question: What is a robot?
questions.options: A machine with a computer inside that does a job by itself | A person wearing a shiny metal costume | Any toy that is made of metal | A machine that can feel happy or sad
questions.correctAnswer: A machine with a computer inside that does a job by itself
questions.explanation: A robot is a machine with a computer inside that can do a job all by itself. It is not a person, and it cannot feel anything.

questions.question: What is a network?
questions.options: A very long electric wire | One computer all on its own | A game you play on a tablet | Two or more computers or devices joined together so they can share
questions.correctAnswer: Two or more computers or devices joined together so they can share
questions.explanation: A network is when two or more computers or devices are joined together — the joining lets them communicate and share.

questions.question: What is the internet?
questions.options: A place in town that you can walk to | The biggest network of all, joining computers all around the world | A computer that lives inside your tablet | A wire that joins two rooms in a house
questions.correctAnswer: The biggest network of all, joining computers all around the world
questions.explanation: The internet is the biggest network in the whole world — lots and lots of computers joined together. Your tablet joins it; it does not hold it.

questions.question: Amina's tablet is joined to the internet, so her videos play and her messages send. What do we call this?
questions.options: asleep | online | broken | offline
questions.explanation: When a device is joined to the internet, we are online. When there is no connection, we are offline.

questions.question: Which of these can join a network?
questions.options: a bicycle | a printer | a football | a wooden chair
questions.explanation: A printer is made to connect, so it can join a network — just like a laptop, a tablet or a phone. A bicycle, a ball or a chair cannot join.

questions.question: A set of steps for doing a job, in the right order, has a special name. What is it?
questions.options: a robot | a network | a pictogram | an algorithm
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job, done in the right order — we follow algorithms every day without knowing the word.

questions.question: Hassan follows his getting-dressed algorithm but puts his shoes on before his socks. What does this muddle show us?
questions.options: Getting dressed needs no steps | The order of the steps matters | The steps were all wrong | Shoes and socks are the same thing
questions.correctAnswer: The order of the steps matters
questions.explanation: We follow the steps of an algorithm from first to last. If we mix up the order, we get a muddle — even if all the steps are right.

questions.question: Layla changes one block in her ScratchJr program so her character takes more steps. What happens to the outcome?
questions.options: Nothing changes at all | The character disappears forever | The outcome changes - the character moves further | The tablet switches itself off
questions.correctAnswer: The outcome changes - the character moves further
questions.explanation: If we change a step, we change the outcome — the outcome just means what happens when the program runs.

questions.question: In ScratchJr, what must you do with your blocks so the whole program runs?
questions.options: Click them together in a row like a jigsaw | Leave a gap between every block | Use only one block at a time | Spread them anywhere on the screen
questions.correctAnswer: Click them together in a row like a jigsaw
questions.explanation: Blocks must click together in a row like a jigsaw — if there is a gap, only the first part runs.

questions.question: What is a mistake in a program called?
questions.options: a block | a bug | a badge | a step
questions.explanation: A mistake in a program is called a bug, and finding and fixing it is called debugging. Everyone makes bugs — even grown-ups who build computer games.

questions.question: An algorithm for making tea says: 1 boil the water, 2 drink the tea, 3 pour the water into the cup. Which step is in the wrong place?
questions.options: Step 3 - you never pour the water | Step 1 - boiling the water should come last | Step 2 - drinking the tea should come last | Nothing is wrong with the order
questions.correctAnswer: Step 2 - drinking the tea should come last
questions.explanation: You cannot drink the tea before the water is poured into the cup! A problem solver finds the wrong step and says where it should go.

questions.question: Yusuf finishes building his tap game, then tries it to check that it works. What is this called?
questions.options: sharing | drawing | sorting | testing
questions.explanation: Testing means trying your game to check that it works. Even the people who make the biggest games test them again and again.

questions.question: Nadia draws a square window with direction steps: right, down, left, and then one more direction. Which direction finishes the square?
questions.options: left | up | right | down
questions.explanation: A square uses the same four little moves — right, down, left, up. The last side goes up, back to where the pencil started.

questions.question: What is data?
questions.options: A kind of computer game | A wire inside a laptop | Information - it can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds | Only very big numbers
questions.correctAnswer: Information - it can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds
questions.explanation: Data is a fancy word for information — it can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds.

questions.question: Sara puts all the red blocks together and all the blue blocks together. What is she doing with her data?
questions.options: throwing it away | sorting it into groups | turning it into sounds | hiding it in a box
questions.explanation: To sort means to put things into groups — things in the same group are the same in some way, like all the red ones together.

questions.question: Bilal asks his friends their favourite fruit and makes one quick mark for each answer. What are these quick counting marks called?
questions.options: full stops | question marks | stickers | tally marks
questions.explanation: A tally mark is a quick way to count — one mark for each answer, so no answer gets lost.

questions.question: In a pictogram, one box stands for one child. Five children like mango. How many boxes should Nadia colour?
questions.explanation: In a pictogram, one box means one thing. If five children like mango, we colour five boxes — one box for each child.

questions.question: Omar's block graph shows favourite pets: cats have 4 blocks, birds have 6 blocks and fish have 2 blocks. Which pet got the most votes?
questions.options: They all got the same | birds | fish | cats
questions.explanation: The longest row of blocks shows the biggest group — birds have 6 blocks, and 6 is more than 4 and 2.

questions.question: Which of these is personal information that you must keep private online?
questions.options: the name of a cartoon | your favourite fruit | your home address | your favourite colour
questions.explanation: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information — never type them into a game, an app or a website.

questions.question: While Leo is playing an online game, something pops up that upsets him. What should he do?
questions.options: Keep it a secret from everyone | Type in his name to make it go away | Stop, leave the page and tell an adult he trusts | Watch it again to be sure
questions.correctAnswer: Stop, leave the page and tell an adult he trusts
questions.explanation: If anything online upsets you, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

questions.question: A player Sara only knows online asks for her school's name and her phone number. What should she do?
questions.options: Send them because the player seems friendly | Promise the player to keep it a secret | Never send them, and tell an adult she trusts | Send only the phone number
questions.correctAnswer: Never send them, and tell an adult she trusts
questions.explanation: A school name and a phone number are personal information. Never send them to someone you only know online — and tell an adult you trust what happened.
